Parks Canada expects to eliminate about 500 full-time-equivalent positions, close 13 park-warden detachments and discontinue its Banff search-and-rescue dog program as part of $145 million in cuts over three years. The agency sent workforce-adjustment notices to 2,917 employees and says it will make individual decisions in the coming weeks. The Canadian Avalanche Rescue Dog Association and British Columbia Search Dog Association have urged the agency to reverse the cancellation, warning it could weaken rescue capacity. Parks Canada says it will shift wardens to a regional model focused on high-risk areas and that wardens can enforce park law without dogs. The associations say they are working on a short-term volunteer response during avalanche season.

items.title: [phys.org] Researchers document sustained sexual bond between Ethiopian bull and male donkey
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

An Italian-led research team documented repeated sexual interactions between a bull and a male donkey on an Ethiopian plateau, describing a selective social bond between the animals. During eight days of observation in March 2026, the bull, Achilles, mounted the donkey, Patroclus, 51 times; 34 mountings involved penetration. The findings appeared Nov. 2 in the journal Current Biology. The pair also licked, rubbed and nuzzled one another, and researchers repeatedly saw them seek each other out despite access to other potential mates. The team cautions that observations of one domesticated pair cannot establish why the behavior occurred or what the animals felt. Dry-season conditions led herders to move them to separate pastures; researchers in Ethiopia are trying to arrange a reunion to observe whether their interactions resume.

items.title: [discovermagazine.com] Tests find coca and alcohol in Inca child mummies, but none of the hallucinogens screened for
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers analyzing hair and nails from eight Inca children sacrificed about 500 years ago found traces of coca in hair and evidence of alcohol in some children, but none of the hallucinogens they tested for. The remains came from mountain sites in Peru and Argentina and belonged to children aged 6 to 14. The findings suggest the substances may have helped prepare children for the physical and emotional strain of journeys to sacrificial sites rather than induce hallucinations, said archaeologist Dagmara Socha of the University of Warsaw. Harmine, a plant compound associated with Amazonian species, was found in a nail from Juanita, a 14-year-old mummy. The team plans further study of the substances and sacred mountain sites.

items.title: [theguardian.com] UN-backed report warns overshooting 1.5C could permanently damage Earth's ice
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A report by 80 scientists convened by the International Cryosphere Climate Initiative and the U.N. Environment Programme warns that even a temporary rise above the Paris Agreement’s 1.5C warming limit could cause lasting losses to glaciers, sea ice and polar ice sheets. Earth has already warmed about 1.3C from preindustrial levels. The authors say any period above 1.5C should be as brief as possible before temperatures fall much further, and identify a long-term target below 1C by 2150. Under current policies, warming is projected to reach about 2.8C, a level the report links to near-total thaw of near-surface permafrost and likely severe disruption to ocean circulation. Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets would continue losing ice even if temperatures later returned to 1.5C, while many ice systems could take centuries or millennia to recover. The report was released ahead of the COP31 climate conference in Turkey.

items.title: [livescience.com] NASA's Swift telescope burns up after nearly 22 years
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory reentered Earth’s atmosphere and burned up over North Sumatra on Nov. 4, ending a nearly 22-year mission. Its observations, including millions of images, remain available for research. A 24-hour ultraviolet exposure of the Andromeda galaxy was assembled from observations made between May and July 2008. NASA said Swift detected about 20,000 ultraviolet sources there, many of them hot stars and star clusters obscured in visible-light views. Swift was designed to turn rapidly toward short-lived cosmic explosions and observe them in optical, ultraviolet and X-ray light. It also alerted other observatories so they could follow events before they faded. The U.S. Space Force said Swift reentered the atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST over North Sumatra. NASA expected most of the spacecraft to burn up, though some pieces may have survived.

items.title: [npr.org] Climate change shifts Arctic greenery, darkens lakes and bleaches coral
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Climate change is altering natural colors across Arctic landscapes, lakes and coral reefs, with shifts linked to warming, permafrost thaw and pollution. A satellite study published in 2020 found greening at about 38% of sampled Arctic sites between 1985 and 2016. Another study found that green-wavelength values in more than 400,000 North American boreal-Arctic lakes fell 15% between 1984 and 2019, indicating darker water. Darker lakes can retain heat longer, while coral bleaching leaves reefs more vulnerable to disease and other stressors. Researchers say thawing permafrost may be darkening lakes as soil mixes into the water.

items.title: [latimes.com] El Niño-linked floods force Southwest evacuations; Arizona declares emergency
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Pacific storm systems brought torrential rain and flooding across the normally arid Southwest, prompting evacuations in Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah. The National Weather Service said El Niño was disrupting weather patterns as the region faced another round of heavy rain. Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs declared a statewide emergency Monday to help local authorities clear roads, repair infrastructure and assist displaced residents. Monitoring and alarm systems detected the changes, and staff took precautions, including moving some products. The incident was part of a wave of attacks on refrigeration systems that disrupted European supermarkets in October. Sweden’s regions said no comparable blood-bank attack had been reported there, but they were reviewing and strengthening cybersecurity protections. French authorities said technical investigations were continuing to determine how the breach occurred, how many devices may have been affected and when the systems could safely return to service.

items.title: [efeagro.com] Hackers raise supermarket freezer temperatures across Europe, spoiling food
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Cyberattacks disrupted refrigeration at grocery stores and other businesses in several European countries overnight into Nov. 2, raising temperatures in some units to 50°C and prompting businesses to discard food or remove it as a precaution. Affected countries included Belgium, Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia, Finland and Luxembourg; reports also described incidents in Italy, though the extent there remains unclear. In Belgium, Delhaize reported refrigeration problems in about 40 stores, Carrefour in 15 and Spar in five. Ireland’s SuperValu reported incidents at 13 stores, while refrigeration supplier Danfoss said at least 17 Dutch businesses were affected. The attackers appear to have remotely changed settings on connected equipment, in some cases activating defrost mode. European Agriculture and Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen described the repeated attacks as an attempt to disrupt food supply and weaken consumer trust, but said food security was not currently threatened. Belgian federal prosecutors opened an investigation, but no group has claimed responsibility and authorities have not established whether the incidents were part of one operation. Italy scheduled a government crisis meeting for Nov. 3 with national cybersecurity and intelligence officials.

items.title: [cisa.gov] U.S. agencies warn hackers are targeting industrial refrigeration controls
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Five U.S. agencies warned on Nov. 5 that hackers are targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems worldwide, including controllers used by grocery stores, hospitals, food producers and transport operators. Attackers may exploit unpatched or internet-accessible devices to change temperatures or defrost settings, or prevent operators from seeing temperature readings. Such attacks could spoil stock, compromise storage safety and damage equipment. The warning follows attacks on European supermarkets on Nov. 2 and an incident that altered refrigeration settings at three French blood-service facilities. The U.S. agencies did not say whether refrigeration systems in the United States had been targeted. They urged operators to remove unnecessary internet access, secure remote connections, update firmware, isolate control systems from business networks and set alerts for unsafe temperature changes.
